title: Genesis 28:10–22
context: Jacob leaves Beersheba toward Haran, sleeps with a stone for a pillow, and dreams of a ladder between earth and heaven. The LORD restates Abraham’s promise, pledges His presence, and Jacob wakes to name the place Bethel—then vows oil, house, and a tenth.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Historic words on Jacob’s ladder and the God of Bethel—so each camp speaks in its own voice on the Mediator who joins heaven and earth.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: The mediation of Christ. He is this ladder: the foot on earth in his human nature, the top in heaven in his divine nature… All the intercourse between heaven and earth since the fall is by this ladder. Christ is the way: all God’s favours come to us, and all our services come to him, by Christ.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the Old Testament (on Gen 28:12)

arminian.quote: It was probably a type of Christ, in whom both worlds meet, and in whom the Divine and human nature are conjoined. The Ladder was set up on the Earth, and the Top of it reached to Heaven; for God was manifested in the Flesh, and in him dwelt all the fullness of the Godhead bodily. … Jesus Christ is the grand connecting medium between heaven and earth, and between God and man. By him God comes down to man; through him man ascends to God.

reformed.quote: It is Christ alone, therefore, who connects heaven and earth: he is the only Mediator who reaches from heaven down to earth: he is the medium through which the fullness of all celestial blessings flows down to us, and through which we, in turn, ascend to God.

That ladder … was a picture of Christ, the way of access between man and God. You will never perceive God in nature, until you have learned to see God in grace. … You must first of all perceive God incarnate in the flesh of Christ, before you will perceive God in the creation which he has made. … When I see Christ, I see God’s new and living way, between my soul and my God, most clear and pleasant.
reformed.source: Sermon 401, “Jacob’s Waking Exclamation,” on Gen 28:16 (21 July 1861)

verses.text: Jacob went out from Beersheba, and went toward Haran.
verses.arminianNotes:
Beersheba to Haran: the blessed heir is on the road, not on a throne. Departure is obedience under pressure.

God can meet a man in transit. The journey is already a response to Isaac’s charge; grace will meet him farther on.
verses.reformedNotes:
The heir of promise exits the land of sojourning toward the east. Moses states the fact without ornament.

Comfort: leaving is not loss of the covenant. The God of Beersheba will prove He is not bound to one well.

verses.text: He came to a certain place, and stayed there all night, because the sun had set. He took one of the stones of the place, and put it under his head, and lay down in that place to sleep.
verses.arminianNotes:
Sunset, a stone, sleep: no inn, no retinue. Need becomes the setting for revelation. Jacob lies down because he must, not because the place looks holy yet.

Arminians notice that God often draws near where we did not plan a sanctuary. Weariness is no barrier to grace that still seeks the fugitive.
verses.reformedNotes:
“A certain place” is unnamed until God names it. Providence times the halt to sundown and a stone pillow.

The heir’s poverty is not evidence of divine absence. The Lord has appointed this hard bed for a vision.

verses.text: He dreamed and saw a stairway set upon the earth, and its top reached to heaven. Behold, the angels of God were ascending and descending on it.
verses.arminianNotes:
Earth and heaven are joined: a ladder, angels going both ways. The fugitive is shown that traffic with God has not been cut off by his exile—or his recent sin.

With Wesley, the ladder images Christ’s mediation, the way of access sincerely opened. Favors come down and services go up by this way, offered to the one who will trust it.
verses.reformedNotes:
The dream is revelation, not indigestion. Angels move on a ladder whose top is heaven; God is about to speak from above it.

Calvin confesses that Christ alone connects heaven and earth. The covenant is founded in the Mediator; Bethel already preaches the One who fills the gap sin made.
verses.keyContrast: Both read the ladder as more than scenery, and both end at Christ. Arminians press an opened way of intercourse with God, sincerely given to the wanderer; Reformed interpreters typically stress that the covenant’s traffic runs only through the appointed Mediator, shown here in figure.

verses.text: Behold, the LORD stood above it, and said, “I am the LORD, the God of Abraham your father, and the God of Isaac. I will give the land you lie on to you and to your offspring.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD stands above the ladder and names Himself: God of Abraham and Isaac. Then He gives the land under Jacob’s body to him and his offspring. Speech interprets the vision.

Wesleyans hear a personal address. The God of the fathers sincerely pledges land to this son; the gift calls for trust from a man who does not yet hold a deed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Mute vision is not left mute. “I am the LORD” anchors Jacob in the God of the fathers; land is granted by oath-speech while he still lies on it as a stranger.

God Himself constitutes Jacob heir. The father’s blessing is now the LORD’s own mouth.

verses.text: Your offspring will be as the dust of the earth, and you will spread abroad to the west, and to the east, and to the north, and to the south. In you and in your offspring, all the families of the earth will be blessed.
verses.arminianNotes:
Dust-many offspring, four-direction spread, and blessing for all families: Abraham’s gospel is restated over a man with a stone pillow. The horizon is the nations.

“All the families of the earth” is a sincere worldwide aim. In Jacob’s offspring—ultimately the Seed—God opens blessing to be received by faith, not a closed clan prize.
verses.reformedNotes:
The Abrahamic formula returns in full: numberless seed, geographic spread, global blessing. God binds the nations’ good to this man’s line.

The promise is as sure as the Speaker. All families will be blessed in the Seed God has appointed; Jacob’s emptiness tonight cannot shrink the oath.
verses.keyContrast: Both hear Genesis 12 restated at Bethel. Arminians emphasize a sincere blessing aimed at all families, to be received by faith; Reformed readers underline that the same worldwide word is God’s effectual covenant in the Seed He will not fail to send.

verses.text: Behold, I am with you, and will keep you, wherever you go, and will bring you again into this land. For I will not leave you until I have done that which I have spoken of to you.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Presence, keeping, homecoming, and a “until” tied to promise: God pledges Himself to a traveling sinner. “Wherever you go” covers Haran, Laban, and the long way back.

Arminians treasure the companionship. Grace goes with Jacob and still calls him to walk in that keeping—presence that comforts and claims.
verses.reformedNotes:
God anticipates the fear of exile: I am with you; I will keep you; I will bring you back; I will not leave you until the promise is done.

The Keeper’s “until” is not a threat of abandonment but a pledge of completion. Jacob’s safety rests on God’s fidelity to His own word.
verses.keyContrast: Both cling to “I am with you.” Arminians typically hear an accompanying grace that Jacob must continue to trust and not treat as automatic; Reformed readers hear an effectual keeper-promise that will not stop until God has done all He said.

verses.text: Jacob awakened out of his sleep, and he said, “Surely the LORD is in this place, and I didn’t know it.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Waking confession: the LORD was here, and Jacob had not known. Revelation uncovers unnoticed presence. Ignorance was no illusion; so is the new recognition.

We sometimes meet God where we did not ask. Grace can surprise a dull traveler and invite him to live awake.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jacob names both the fact and his prior blindness. God was in the place before Jacob named it holy.

The initiative remains the LORD’s appearing. Jacob’s knowledge is gift; the place did not become God’s house because Jacob guessed well.

verses.text: He was afraid, and said, “How awesome this place is! This is none other than God’s house, and this is the gate of heaven.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Fear and awe, not casual warmth: house of God, gate of heaven. Nearness humbles. Access is not imaginary, and it is not casual.

The gate is open in mercy, and the holiness of the place still bows the sinner who stumbles into it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Dread and comfort meet at Bethel. “Gate of heaven” is Jacob’s name for the opened access the ladder showed.

Majesty that would terrify also, in the Mediator, admits. The house is God’s before it is Jacob’s shrine.

verses.text: Jacob rose up early in the morning, and took the stone that he had put under his head, and set it up for a pillar, and poured oil on its top.
verses.arminianNotes:
Dawn turns the pillow into a pillar; oil marks it. Memory becomes worship. Jacob answers revelation with a concrete act.

Grace received seeks a response. The stone is not a rival god; it is a witness that this man will not pretend the night was only a dream.
verses.reformedNotes:
Early rising, pillar, oil: consecration of a memorial, not the carving of an idol. The same stone that served sleep now serves testimony.

Worship here is response to the word already spoken. Jacob does not create the presence; he marks where God has spoken.

verses.text: He called the name of that place Bethel, but the name of the city was Luz at the first.
verses.arminianNotes:
Bethel—“house”—overwrites Luz in Jacob’s mouth. Naming is theology: this spot is interpreted by the night, not by the town’s old label.

Grace teaches us to rename ordinary ground. What was merely Luz can become, in encounter, a house of God for the one who received the vision.
verses.reformedNotes:
Two names stand: Luz in the map, Bethel in the revelation. Moses records both so later readers will know the city did not yet live by Jacob’s title.

The place is named Bethel because God appeared there. The house is His; Jacob’s word only confesses what the dream disclosed.

verses.text: Jacob vowed a vow, saying, “If God will be with me, and will keep me in this way that I go, and will give me bread to eat, and clothing to put on,
verses.arminianNotes:
The vow begins with “If”—not haggling so much as taking God at the night’s word: presence, keeping, bread, clothes. Need is confessed without shame.

Arminians catch a man binding himself to gratitude if the promised help arrives. The conditions track God’s own pledges; faith answers with a vowed life.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jacob’s “if” restates the promise God just made: with you, keep you, provide. The vow is appendage to the oracle, not a bribe to make God kind.

The grammar sounds conditional, yet the content is borrowed from verse 15. The heir clings to the Keeper’s terms.

verses.text: so that I come again to my father’s house in peace, and the LORD will be my God,
verses.arminianNotes:
Home in peace, then “the LORD will be my God.” Jacob aims the vow at belonging, not at a mere safe trip. The God of the fathers is to be his God.

This is a responsible yielding. Grace has spoken; Jacob pledges personal allegiance if he is brought home—a true “my God,” not inherited slogan only.
verses.reformedNotes:
Return in peace is the promise’s earthly shape; “the LORD will be my God” is covenant language. Jacob takes the God of Abraham as his own.

God will be Jacob’s God because God has already named Himself so. The vow confesses what electing mercy has begun.
verses.keyContrast: Both refuse to reduce the vow to a bargain for groceries. Arminians hear Jacob’s responsible “then… my God” as grace-enabled allegiance; Reformed interpreters usually hear the vow as faith clinging to a God who has already claimed him.

verses.text: then this stone, which I have set up for a pillar, will be God’s house. Of all that you will give me I will surely give a tenth to you.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Pillar as God’s house, and a tenth of all God gives: worship and open-handed return. Jacob plans a future at this stone and a habit of giving.

Received mercy trains generosity. The tenth is response, not purchase. What God gives can be given back in thanks.
verses.reformedNotes:
The stone will be God’s house; the tenth will acknowledge the Giver of “all that you will give me.” Even the tithe assumes God’s prior giving.

Jacob’s religion at Bethel is built on gift. House and tenth are signs that the Keeper who promised will also supply what He is owed in gratitude.
